title: SCADA Historian Integration: What It Is and How It Works
summary: Discover how SCADA historian integration works, why it matters for industrial operations, and how modern time-series platforms fit into the picture.
body_markdown:
Summary


Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) systems are real-time plant command and control systems. While some may include historical data capabilities, organizations often need to retain larger volumes of telemetry, perform complex analysis, and make operational data accessible across the enterprise.


Table of Contents


Building more efficient and reliable facilities can be a moving target, but in order to plan for progress, organizations require the ability to analyze historical data. For companies with SCADA systems, one way to enable this is integrating their data historian with a time series database.


Modern platforms like **InfluxDB** streamline integration with superior tagging, high-speed ingestion, and query performance, giving you the speed, scale, and flexibility you need for real-time dashboards, edge-to-cloud telemetry, and industrial AI models.


Modern industrial facilities, like water treatment and manufacturing plants, run on continuous streams of high-frequency telemetry. Programmable logic controllers (PLCs), remote terminal units (RTUs), and smart sensors log critical information every second, enabling essential infrastructure like power utilities to literally “keep the lights on.”


But many organizations have a major operational problem: segregated silos. They have supervisory control systems that only support short-term data storage and that only offer flat files or relational databases with inadequate analytics performance.


[SCADA](https://www.influxdata.com/glossary/SCADA-supervisory-control-and-data-acquisition/?utm_source=website&utm_medium=direct&utm_campaign=scada_historian_integration&utm_content=blog) historian integration addresses these issues by bridging SCADA networks and dedicated process historians or time series databases.


Instead of overloading primary control systems with complex queries or shoehorning time series data into a relational database, this solution gives supervisory data a purpose-built place to live.


## What’s the difference between SCADA and a data historian?


Why do we need to integrate these two systems—SCADA and[data historians](https://www.influxdata.com/glossary/data-historian/?utm_source=website&utm_medium=direct&utm_campaign=scada_historian_integration&utm_content=blog) —in the first place? They’re both components of your[operational technology](https://www.influxdata.com/blog/upgrade-iot-ot-tech-stack-replace-legacy-data-historians-influxdb/?utm_source=website&utm_medium=direct&utm_campaign=scada_historian_integration&utm_content=blog) (OT) stack and manage time series metrics from field devices. Why can’t they do their jobs alone?


#### Understanding SCADA Systems


SCADA systems are real-time command centers for industrial operations. They continuously communicate with PLCs and RTUs to provide operators with the UIs and alerts they need to manage their systems.


We can summarize SCADA systems this way:


- **Primary Function** : Real-time monitoring, device state control, and alarm handling.
- **Time Horizon** : Sub-second to several seconds.
- **Storage Engine** : Highly transactional, spanning memory buffers and relational databases intended for state checks rather than trend analysis or history.


Vendors optimize their SCADA platforms for low-latency operations and control. Using them to store months or years of telemetry degrades performance, and they still fall short of providing comprehensive queries and reports.


#### Understanding Process Historians


A[process historian](https://www.influxdata.com/blog/influxdb-modern-process-historian/?utm_source=website&utm_medium=direct&utm_campaign=scada_historian_integration&utm_content=blog) is a time series data platform that specializes in ingesting and storing large volumes of industrial telemetry over extended periods. Rather than focusing on controlling devices and managing alerts, it provides the historical storage that SCADA systems lack.


We can contrast historians with SCADA like this:


- **Primary Function** : High-speed and high-volume[data ingestion](https://docs.influxdata.com/influxdb3/clustered/write-data/best-practices/data-lifecycle/?utm_source=website&utm_medium=direct&utm_campaign=scada_historian_integration&utm_content=blog) and analytical queries.
- **Time Horizon** : Months and years of continuous history.
- **Storage Engine** : Time series databases with column-based indexing for fast querying and analysis.


#### SCADA vs. Historian at a Glance


Feature SCADA System Process Historian


**Primary Role** Real-time plant control and operation Long-term operational analysis and reporting


**Data Time Frame** Current state (seconds to minutes) Historical trends (weeks to years)


**Storage Architecture** Short-term buffers/transactional databases Time series databases


**Data Ingestion** High-frequency polling and alarm state changes Continuous time series streams


**Primary Users** Plant operators, field technicians Process engineers, data scientists, management


## Why integrate SCADA systems and data historians?


Now that we’ve covered the differences between these two OT components, let’s see why so many organizations have benefited from connecting them. This integration addresses a number of fundamental operational and strategic challenges:


#### Offload Primary Control Infrastructure


When you attempt to run long-term queries or historical reports against a SCADA database, you risk resource contention.


Time series requests lead to heavy read operations, especially using a database ill-suited for[time series analysis](https://www.influxdata.com/what-is-time-series-data/?utm_source=website&utm_medium=direct&utm_campaign=scada_historian_integration&utm_content=blog) , often causing UIs to lag, delayed commands to controllers, and missed alarms.


By offloading data logging, storage, and analysis to a historian, you free up your SCADA system to perform its job: low-latency, real-time control and monitoring.


#### Unlocking High-Resolution Reporting and Analysis


SCADA systems excel at telling you what’s happening now, but they lack the context and tools to explain why an anomaly happened in the past. You need an integrated process historian to capture time series data for root cause analysis, predictive maintenance modeling, and establishing process baselines.


#### Establish Regulatory Compliance


Heavily regulated sectors like water management, power generation, and pharmaceuticals mandate strict proof of operating conditions. This means maintaining complete audit trails for critical data such as key sensor levels and events.


SCADA systems are not equipped to do this; historians are.


#### Drive IT and IOT Convergence


Industrial data is valuable, but you can’t harness that value if the data stays trapped on the plant floor. When you integrate SCADA with a historian, you gain a structured interface between your OT environment and your corporate information technology (IT) network.


Historians and time series databases make operational data available to enterprise applications while maintaining OT/IT separation through appropriate network segmentation, access controls, and secure data-transfer mechanisms.


## How SCADA historian integration works


SCADA historian integration converts signals from physical equipment into structured data you can use for reports, queries, and audit trails.


#### The Telemetry Pipeline


Integration begins at the edge of the operational network. Collectors (services that run on SCADA gateways or edge devices) sample data tags from field devices and create a continuous data stream. Tools like[Telegraf](https://www.influxdata.com/time-series-platform/telegraf/?utm_source=website&utm_medium=direct&utm_campaign=scada_historian_integration&utm_content=blog) can simplify this process of integrating and collecting data.


Depending on the underlying protocol, data collection follows one of these two models:


##### Polling (Request-Response)


The collector queries PLCs or SCADA servers at regular intervals to fetch current tag values.


##### Publish-Subscribe


IOT devices or gateways publish telemetry when a value changes outside a designated threshold or when a periodic heartbeat is reached. This model reduces network traffic compared to polling.


#### Buffering and Store-and-Forward Resilience


Transient disconnects, maintenance outages, and latency spikes are unavoidable. Even the most resilient and best designed networks experience these issues. But you can’t afford to lose data, especially if you’re subject to regulatory compliance.


To guarantee zero data loss, integration architectures rely on store-and-forward mechanisms. When an edge collector loses connection to the central historian, it diverts its data stream to secure storage, usually a local disk buffer. When connectivity returns, it backfills the time series data from the buffer.


#### Metadata and Contextualization


You can’t do much with time series data without context. During ingestion, the integration layer enriches your data streams with standardized metadata attributes:


- **Asset Hierarchy Alignment** : Tags that map to logical frameworks like the ISA-95 standard (Enterprise -> Site -> Area -> Line -> Cell -> Asset).
- **Engineering Units & Data Types** : Tags that define the unit of measure an entry corresponds to.
- **Quality Flags** : Health status codes denoting the quality of the attached data.


## Best practices and pitfalls


When you begin SCADA historian integration, you’re creating a data repository you’ll want to use for a long time to come. Here’s a set of best practices and pitfalls to keep in mind as you start the project.


#### 1. Establish Tag Naming Conventions Early


Before you begin storing data in your historian, establish a consistent tag naming taxonomy that aligns with both your physical system and industry standards like ISA 95. Inconsistent tagging created on the fly will lead to confusion, inefficient queries, and expensive technical debt.


#### 2. Configure Robust Store-and-Forward Buffers


Create your store-and-forward buffers based on worst-case network scenarios. Your edge collectors should be able to store data for days, not just hours. This means sizing the collectors for enough disk space to store that data, and allowing for potential growth.


#### 3. Avoid Stripping Operational Metadata


Data historians and[time series databases](https://www.influxdata.com/time-series-database/?utm_source=website&utm_medium=direct&utm_campaign=scada_historian_integration&utm_content=blog) like[InfluxDB](https://www.influxdata.com/products/influxdb-overview/?utm_source=website&utm_medium=direct&utm_campaign=scada_historian_integration&utm_content=blog) rely on tags for querying data, and they do an excellent job compressing and storing them. So, avoid the urge to discard key information like engineering units, quality flags, and asset associations.


#### 4. Be Mindful of Network Bandwidth Constraints


Streaming raw, uncompressed telemetry directly over satellite, cellular, or WAN links risks saturating network connections and incurring unnecessary data charges. Design edge processing, filtering, and time series compression into your telemetry collection from the beginning.


## Modernize your industrial telemetry pipeline


Integrating SCADA systems, industrial historians, and modern time series databases enables organizations to extend operational telemetry beyond plant-floor monitoring and control. The right architecture depends on existing capabilities and new analytical requirements.


A dedicated pipeline that connects isolated real-time telemetry to the proper storage provides operational insights while keeping your supervisory infrastructure safe.


Managing continuous streams of high-resolution OT data shouldn’t be constrained by rigid tag limits or slow query engines. Find the best process historian for your needs before you start your integration project.

## FAQs


What is a historian in a SCADA system? A process historian is a specialized time series database storage engine designed to ingest, compress, and store high-frequency telemetry from a plant floor. It indexes data from PLCs, RTUs, and sensors over extended periods of time. Unlike standard SQL databases, a historian is purpose-built to handle continuous, high-volume sensor streams and perform long-term analysis over months or years of history.


What is the difference between SCADA and a historian? A Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) system functions as a real-time command center for a plant, while a historian archives data streams for querying and reporting. SCADA is focused on sub-second monitoring, device control, and alarms. It’s limited to short-term memory buffers and transactional databases, so it’s not well suited for querying. A process historian specializes in high-speed data ingestion and long-term data retention. It’s the foundation for root-cause analysis, predictive maintenance, and regulatory auditing since it is purpose-built for fast and powerful queries.


What is SCADA integration? SCADA integration (specifically SCADA-historian integration) is the process of building a secure pipeline between real-time control networks and enterprise-level storage or cloud analytics engines. It involves collecting telemetry at the edge, buffering data locally using store-and-forward (SaF) mechanisms to prevent loss during outages, and enriching raw signals with standardized metadata. This integration offloads query traffic from SCADA and bridges plant-floor OT systems and corporate IT environments.


How does SCADA historian integration support industrial AI and physical AI? Industrial AI and Physical AI depend on accurate, timely operational data to understand how equipment behaves and respond to changing conditions. SCADA historian integration makes real-time and historical telemetry available to AI applications for anomaly detection, predictive maintenance, process optimization, and digital twins. For Physical AI applications, such as autonomous robots and intelligent manufacturing systems, this data provides additional context about equipment conditions, operating history, and the outcomes of previous actions. Modern time series databases like InfluxDB support these applications by capturing high-resolution telemetry and making it available for AI model training, inference, and operational analysis..
